claims.text: Substrate preheating during additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloys will improve dimensional precision.
Substrate preheating during additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloys will improve mechanical integrity.
Substrate preheating reduces thermal gradients and associated residual stresses that cause fabrication-induced defects.
Room-temperature-substrate printing of high-entropy alloys produces significant thermal gradients.
Thermal gradients in the as-printed material induce residual stresses, microsegregation, porosity, and dimensional distortion.
An optimized substrate-preheating temperature is estimated to lie between 600 and 800 degrees Celsius, depending on alloy composition.
Reducing thermal gradients decreases residual-stress accumulation.
Reduced thermal gradients enable more controlled microstructural evolution and thereby mitigate porosity and cracking.
Maintaining an elevated substrate temperature during deposition lowers the cooling rate and thermal gradients between layers.
Lower interlayer thermal gradients minimize thermal stresses responsible for dimensional distortion and defect formation.
Elevated-temperature deposition produces more uniform solidification that refines the microstructure and enhances mechanical properties.
Preheated samples will have less dimensional distortion than room-temperature-substrate controls.
Preheated samples will have lower porosity and less cracking than room-temperature-substrate controls.
Preheated samples will have higher tensile strength and fracture toughness than room-temperature-substrate controls.
Rapid cooling under room-temperature-substrate conditions produces high thermal gradients, residual stresses, dimensional inaccuracies, defects, and suboptimal mechanical performance.
Excessively high substrate-preheating temperatures may cause unintended grain growth or altered melting dynamics.
The effect of substrate preheating may vary among high-entropy-alloy compositions because their elevated-temperature phase-stability limits differ.
